patches.old: Premise addressed: Capability gains will be gradual and visible. States the contrary expectation without engaging any argument for gradual takeoff. Earlier than the CFAI passage (2001-06-15) and his SL4 answer of 2001-01-24.
patches.new: Premise addressed: Capability gains will be gradual and visible. The opening paragraph states the contrary expectation. Later in the same message (section “Webmind’s awakening”, “How fast would a Webmind wake up?”), answering Goertzel’s view that others would observe a “real AI” and play catch-up, he argues that once an AI can enhance itself independently of its programmers it can “redesign itself radically in accelerated subjective time and walk out as a transhuman”, passing from a prehuman to a transhuman state before observation and catch-up would matter. This records the argument, not its validity. Earlier than the CFAI passage (2001-06-15) and his SL4 answer of 2001-01-24.

old.rationale: Under the message-level rule, the passage states the contrary conclusion without giving a reason against the premise that capability gains will be gradual and visible, even when read with its message or dialogue turn.

new.rationale: Under the message-level rule, the message gives a reason against the premise that capability gains will be gradual and visible: an AI that improves itself independently, in accelerated subjective time, could pass from a prehuman to a transhuman state before others observe it and catch up.

The message argues that the forces of a Singularity are vast and dominated by positive feedback, and that superintelligent action will be too fast to notice once it can be noticed at all. It does not explicitly address a recognisable warning before danger, failures first seen in weaker systems, or action on a warning, so it is recorded as context. It was recorded as contesting the proposition, and headlined as the earliest located contesting text, until the cross-family audit sample of 2026-11-02 (review/cross-family-audit-sample-2026-11-02.md, item 117).

old.rationale: Under the message-level rule, the passage states the contrary conclusion without giving a reason against the premise that there will be a recognisable, consensus-forming signal in time to act, even when read with its message or dialogue turn.

patches.new: Argues that superintelligent action will be too fast to notice; it does not explicitly claim that no recognisable warning will come before danger, that failures will not first appear in weaker systems, or that a warning would not lead to effective action.

row.subject: turing-c1951-heretical-theory
row.statement: Alan Turing’s lecture typescript “Intelligent Machinery, a Heretical Theory” (c. 1951) says that once the machine thinking method had started it would not take long to outstrip human powers, and that at some stage “we should have to expect the machines to take control”, as mentioned in Butler’s Erewhon.

time.note: Approximate year: the King’s College catalogue dates the lecture typescript (AMT/B/4), a lecture to the ’51 Society at Manchester, c. 1951. No lecture day is established. The wording is dated by the typescript, not by its printing in Philosophia Mathematica (September 1996).

row.qualification: A conditional forecast: the lecture assumes that thinking machines can be made. The reference to Erewhon is the typescript’s own citation of Butler; it is not evidence of influence and does not carry over Butler’s other arguments. The same sentence is recorded on A1 in the superintelligence collection. Later than Butler’s letter of 1863, which holds the earliest located role.

row.locator: Typescript p. 10, final sentence (AMT/B/4/16, scan 16); the same sentence on carbon p. 101 (AMT/B/4/6, scan 6)
row.passage: At some stage therefore we should have to expect the machines to take control, in the way that is mentioned in Samuel Butler's 'Erewhon'.
row.note: Read on the archive’s scan, typescript p. 10 (scan 16), compared with carbon p. 101 (scan 6), by the Turing 1951 lead report of 2026-11-02 (research/turing-1951-lead-2026-11-02/report.md, B4-P1), which gives the passage verbatim; that report, by a model of another family, is the cross-family pass for this record. The session admitting it re-read the passage on the same scan on 2026-11-02. The scan has no text layer. Admitted by the maintainer’s decision of 2026-11-02. No human editorial review.

row.subject: turing-1951-can-digital-computers-think
row.statement: Alan Turing’s broadcast script “Can Digital Computers Think?” (1951) asks where we should be if a machine thought more intelligently than we do, says that even if machines were kept subservient we should as a species feel greatly humbled, and compares the possibility of being superseded by the pig or the rat.

time.note: The King’s College catalogue identifies the annotated script (AMT/B/5) with the BBC Third Programme broadcast of 15 May 1951; the script’s composition and annotations are not dated to that day, and it is not a recording of what was said.

row.qualification: The script introduces these points as features that make the idea of a thinking machine unpleasant, in a paragraph on irrational opposition to it. The supersession it names is by pigs or rats, not machines. Do not substitute the stronger prediction of the Heretical Theory lecture for this script.

thought.missing: Considers machines more intelligent than people and keeping them subservient; it does not state that machines would replace or succeed humans as the dominant intelligence.

row.locator: Script p. 6a (AMT/B/5/7, scan 7), paragraph on irrational opposition to the idea
